body:
How rocks preserve the Earth's history

Rocks contain physical and chemical evidence of the conditions under which they formed. Their composition, structure, position and fossil content allow geologists to reconstruct events that occurred long before human history.

The age of a rock is not necessarily the same as the age of the landform in which it occurs. An ancient rock may have been uplifted into a mountain during a much younger geological event.

Rock types and their geological significance

Rock typeFormationExamples
IgneousCooling and solidification of molten materialGranite, basalt
SedimentaryAccumulation and consolidation of sediments, or chemical and biological depositionSandstone, shale, limestone
MetamorphicTransformation of existing rocks through heat, pressure or chemically active fluids, without complete meltingMarble, slate, gneiss

Igneous rocks may preserve evidence of ancient volcanic activity or the cooling of magma underground. Sedimentary rocks frequently preserve information about former environments, while metamorphic rocks provide evidence of changes caused by geological processes such as burial and mountain building.

Fossils and their significance

A fossil is a preserved remain, impression or trace of an organism that lived in the geological past.

Fossils include bones, shells, teeth, leaf impressions, footprints, eggs and other traces of ancient organisms. They occur most commonly in sedimentary rocks because deposition can bury and preserve biological material.

High temperatures associated with molten material generally destroy organic remains. Similarly, intense metamorphism may alter or destroy fossils that were originally present in sedimentary rocks.

Fossils help geologists identify the relative ages of rock formations, reconstruct ancient environments and trace changes in living organisms and continental positions.

Index fossils

An index fossil belongs to an organism that existed during a relatively short geological interval but had a wide geographical distribution. Recognisable index fossils are particularly useful for comparing the ages of rock layers in separate regions.

For example, selected ammonite species are useful in identifying and comparing marine sedimentary formations of Mesozoic age.

Relative and numerical dating

Relative dating

Relative dating establishes whether one geological event or rock formation is older or younger than another. It does not necessarily establish an age in years.

The principle of superposition states that in a normal sequence of deposited layers that has not been overturned, the lower layers are older than the layers above them.

Folding, faulting and other geological disturbances can complicate this relationship. The simple rule must therefore be applied with attention to the condition of the rock layers.

Numerical dating

Numerical dating, often called absolute dating, estimates geological ages in years. Radiometric dating uses the predictable decay of radioactive isotopes to estimate the time since a suitable mineral or rock formed or underwent a significant geological change.

Different dating methods are appropriate for different materials and age ranges. Ancient rocks and meteorites can be studied using long-lived radioactive isotopes, whereas radiocarbon dating is suitable for relatively recent organic material and cannot determine the age of the Earth.

Determining the age of the Earth

Very ancient terrestrial rocks have been repeatedly altered, eroded or recycled through geological processes. Consequently, the oldest surviving rock does not necessarily represent the time when the entire planet formed.

Radiometric studies of meteorites, together with evidence from terrestrial and lunar materials, provide the basis for the accepted estimate of approximately 4.54 billion years for the age of the Earth.

Prelims focus

  • Fossils are most commonly preserved in sedimentary rocks.
  • Index fossils help correlate rock formations of similar geological age.
  • Superposition places older beds below younger beds in an undisturbed sequence.
  • Relative dating establishes chronological order.
  • Radiometric dating estimates numerical ages through radioactive decay.
  • Meteorites provide important evidence for estimating the Earth's age.

Trap: Radiocarbon dating cannot be used to determine the Earth's age of billions of years.

[References: NCERT, Our Environment, Class 7, Chapter 2, Inside Our Earth, section on rocks and minerals; US Geological Survey, Geologic Time: Age of the Earth and Introduction to Geologic Time; US National Park Service, Geologic Principles: Superposition and Original Horizontality; US National Park Service, Geologic Timescale, Geologic Dating Techniques, and Numeric Ages. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Rocks, Fossils and Evidence of Geological Age

body:
Development of continental landmasses

As the early Earth cooled, a solid crust developed above its hotter interior. Over geological time, repeated melting, cooling, deformation and recycling of rocky material contributed to the development and growth of continental crust.

Continental crust is generally thicker and less dense than oceanic crust. Oceanic crust is predominantly basaltic, while continental crust has a more varied composition and contains substantial amounts of relatively silica-rich rocks.

Ancient continental regions have survived for billions of years, although their positions, shapes and boundaries have changed repeatedly.

Wegener's Continental Drift Theory

In 1912, the German scientist Alfred Wegener presented the Continental Drift Theory. He proposed that continents now separated by oceans had formerly been joined together and subsequently moved apart.

According to this broad reconstruction, the major continental landmasses were once united in a supercontinent called Pangaea.

TermGeological meaning
PangaeaAncient supercontinent containing the principal continental landmasses
PanthalassaVast ocean surrounding Pangaea
LaurasiaNorthern continental assemblage, including much of present North America, Europe and Asia
GondwanalandSouthern continental assemblage, including present South America, Africa, India, Antarctica and Australia
TethysAncient marine region lying between the northern and southern continental assemblages

Pangaea assembled during the late Paleozoic and began breaking apart approximately 200 million years ago, near the beginning of the Jurassic Period. Continued fragmentation and continental movement eventually produced the broad arrangement of continents and oceans seen today.

Gondwana had existed as a continental assemblage before Pangaea formed. Therefore, the familiar school-level division of Pangaea into Laurasia and Gondwanaland describes a broad stage of continental history rather than the original creation of Gondwana.

Evidence supporting continental movement

Matching continental margins

The eastern margin of South America and the western margin of Africa show a notable geographical correspondence. Their submerged continental margins provide a better indication of their former relationship than modern shorelines alone.

Similar rocks and geological structures

Rock formations and geological structures of comparable age occur on continents now separated by the Atlantic Ocean. Their similarities support the interpretation that these continental regions were formerly connected.

Distribution of fossils

Fossils of the same ancient organisms occur across widely separated southern continents. Their distribution is consistent with former connections between these landmasses.

  • Glossopteris: An extinct seed plant whose fossils occur in several former Gondwana regions, including India, South America, Africa, Antarctica and Australia.
  • Mesosaurus: An extinct aquatic reptile whose fossils are known from southern Africa and South America.
  • Lystrosaurus: An extinct land-dwelling vertebrate whose fossils occur in India, southern Africa and Antarctica.

Evidence of ancient glaciation

Ancient glacial deposits occur in several Gondwana regions, including areas that now experience warm climates. Their distribution and the directions indicated by glacial markings become easier to explain when the southern continents are reconstructed in their former positions.

From continental drift to plate tectonics

Wegener provided important evidence for continental movement, but the mechanism he proposed was inadequate to explain how continents could move across the Earth.

The subsequent development of plate tectonics supplied a more complete explanation. The Earth's lithosphere is divided into rigid plates that move slowly relative to one another. A plate can carry continental crust, oceanic crust or both.

Continents consequently change their positions as parts of moving lithospheric plates. Where plates separate, new oceanic basins can develop. Where continental plates converge, mountain building may occur.

Continental drift describes the movement of continents. Plate tectonics explains that the moving units are lithospheric plates, rather than continents moving independently through oceanic crust.

Prelims focus

  • Alfred Wegener presented Continental Drift Theory in 1912.
  • Pangaea was a supercontinent; Panthalassa was its surrounding ocean.
  • Peninsular India belonged to Gondwanaland.
  • The fragmentation of Pangaea began around 200 million years ago.
  • Matching rock formations, fossils and ancient glacial deposits support continental movement.
  • Plate tectonics provides the modern explanation for continental movement.

Trap: Pangaea was not the first solid land to form on the Earth; continental rocks existed long before it assembled.

[References: NCERT, Fundamentals of Physical Geography, Class 11, Chapter 4, Distribution of Oceans and Continents, sections on Continental Drift, Evidence and Plate Tectonics; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Geography, Standard 11, 2020 reprint, Chapter 5, Continents and Oceans, pp. 30–35; US Geological Survey, Wegener's Puzzling Continental Drift Evidence; US Geological Survey, This Dynamic Earth: The Himalayas. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]

title: Formation and Movement of Continents

body:
India's ancient continental foundation

The Indian subcontinent contains rocks formed during widely different geological intervals. Its major landforms therefore cannot be assigned a single geological age or a single process of formation.

The Peninsular Plateau contains some of India's oldest surviving continental rocks. Much of its geological foundation consists of ancient igneous and metamorphic rocks dating from the Precambrian.

The long geological history of these rocks has involved repeated deformation, mineral formation, uplift, weathering and erosion. Ancient crystalline rocks of Peninsular India are associated with several important metallic mineral deposits.

The Aravalli region

The Aravalli mountain system is associated with ancient Precambrian geological formations. Its hills have undergone prolonged erosion and are much older in geological origin than the Himalayan mountain system.

Related ancient geological formations extend into northeastern and eastern Gujarat.

Gondwana and the formation of coal deposits

During the geological history of Gondwana, extensive vegetation accumulated in sedimentary basins. Burial beneath additional sediments, followed by compression, heating and chemical changes over geological time, transformed much of this organic material into coal.

India's important Gondwana coal-bearing formations are predominantly associated with the late Paleozoic, especially the Permian. They contain a major share of India's coal resources.

Important Gondwana coalfield regions include the Damodar, Mahanadi and Godavari valleys. The Damodar Valley contains coalfields such as Jharia, Raniganj and Bokaro.

Younger coal deposits also occur in India. These are commonly described in older textbooks as Tertiary coal deposits. They must be distinguished from the much older Gondwana coal-bearing formations.

The northward movement of India

Peninsular India formed part of the southern continental assemblage called Gondwanaland. As Gondwana fragmented, the Indian landmass separated from other southern continental regions and moved northwards.

During much of this movement, the Indian landmass was separated from Eurasia by the ancient Tethys marine region.

Formation of the Deccan Traps

While the Indian landmass was moving northwards, extensive volcanic eruptions occurred across parts of western and central India.

The principal eruptions took place approximately 66 million years ago, around the transition from the Cretaceous Period to the Paleogene Period.

Large quantities of lava spread over extensive areas and solidified into successive basalt layers. These formations are known as the Deccan Traps.

The characteristic step-like appearance of many trap landscapes results from erosion acting on successive layers of volcanic rock. Weathering of basalt has also contributed to the formation of extensive black soils in the Deccan region.

The Deccan Traps are considerably younger than the ancient Precambrian foundation of Peninsular India.

Formation of the Himalayas

During the Cenozoic Era, the Indian Plate collided with the Eurasian Plate. Major Himalayan mountain building is commonly placed around 40–50 million years ago in school-level geological explanations, although the detailed timing of collision and uplift remains a subject of research.

Compression caused extensive folding, faulting, crustal thickening and uplift. Sediments deposited in and around the former Tethys marine region became incorporated into the developing mountain system.

The Himalayas are therefore described as young fold mountains compared with older mountain systems such as the Aravallis. India and Eurasia continue to converge, and Himalayan geological activity continues.

The occurrence of marine fossils in Himalayan rocks can be explained by the uplift of rocks originally formed in marine environments.

Development of the Northern Plains

The uplift and erosion of the Himalayas supplied enormous quantities of sediment to rivers. Rivers draining both the Himalayan and Peninsular regions deposited material in the extensive basin lying between the Himalayas and the Peninsular Plateau.

The accumulation of these sediments over geological time produced the great alluvial plains of northern India.

Much of the widespread near-surface alluvium belongs to the geologically recent Quaternary Period, and sediment deposition continues in active river environments.

Relative ages of major Indian geological features

Prelims focus

  • Precambrian: ancient Peninsular Indian rocks and Aravalli geological formations.
  • Late Paleozoic, especially Permian: major Gondwana coal-bearing formations.
  • Approximately 66 million years ago: principal Deccan Trap eruptions.
  • Cenozoic: collision of India with Eurasia and major Himalayan uplift.
  • Quaternary: extensive younger alluvial deposits in the Northern Plains.
  • Deccan Trap basalt is igneous; river alluvium is deposited sediment.

Trap: The ancient geological foundation of Peninsular India and the volcanic rocks of the Deccan Traps did not form during the same geological interval.

[References: NCERT, Contemporary India I, Class 9, Chapter 2, Physical Features of India, Peninsular Plateau and Northern Plain sections; NCERT, India: Physical Environment, Class 11, Chapter 2, Structure and Physiography, pp. 8–10; NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, Chapter 7, Mineral and Energy Resources, pp. 78–80; US Geological Survey, This Dynamic Earth: The Himalayas; International Union of Geological Sciences, Deccan Traps Geoheritage Site, Geological Description; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Deccan Traps at Panchgani and Mahabaleshwar, Tentative List, Geological Description. Online sources consulted 27 November 2026.]
